prime.problem: A model gives a probability for every token in its vocabulary. Always taking the top one makes every sample identical, but sampling from all of them lets the long tail of unlikely junk tokens in, and over a program of 100+ tokens one bad pick is often enough to break it.
prime.fits: It builds on drawing one outcome from a probability distribution (the toolkit's sampling card) and on temperature, which reshapes that distribution. Top-p is the other half: it cuts the tail before the draw. The structured-outputs course comes back to it when a grammar mask and a top-p cut meet.
expect: sorting by probability and a running total
the nucleus: the smallest set reaching p
prime.goal: Apply a top-p cut by hand to any next-token distribution, and explain why a cutoff set by probability mass adapts to the model's confidence where a fixed k can't.

attend: In the bar chart, why does the cut land after evens rather than after s, and what exact rule decides it?
After the cut, what do you divide by, and why does the order of the five survivors stay the same?
How many tokens would the nucleus hold if the model gave one token 0.97? What does that say about top-p vs a fixed k?
Why do Codex's samples need variety for pass@k, and why is that exactly what greedy decoding destroys?
Codex pairs p = 0.95 with temperature 0.2 or 0.8. Which knob reshapes the distribution and which one removes tokens?

must: Sort tokens by probability → add them up until the running total first reaches p → that smallest set is the nucleus → everything below the cut gets probability 0 → the long tail of junk can't be sampled

The cut is set by probability mass, not by a count → a confident model reaches p with 1–2 tokens and an unsure one needs many → the nucleus shrinks and grows with confidence, where top-k keeps k tokens either way

Kept tokens are divided by their total (0.96 here) → their ratios don't change, only their scale → the draw is still random among plausible tokens → samples differ from each other, which pass@k needs, without the junk that breaks long programs

Temperature reshapes the whole distribution first → top-p then cuts its tail → low T concentrates mass so fewer tokens reach p, and high T spreads it so more survive → the two knobs together set how diverse the samples are
elevated: Pure sampling risks the tail at every token → if 4% of the mass sat below the cut at each of 100 steps, a program would dodge the tail every time with probability 0.96100 ≈ 1.7% → cutting the tail matters more the longer the output
reference: Codex's setting: p = 0.95 on every sampled evaluation (Chen et al. 2021, §3.2)
the paper's temperature optima: about 0.2 for pass@1 and 0.8 for pass@100
the original name and paper: nucleus sampling, Holtzman et al. 2020

compress.prompt: From memory, write top-p as a chain of four arrows (sort → running total → cut → rescale and draw), then one sentence on why it beats top-k and one on what it does not do.
checklist: sort next-token probabilities from highest to lowest
keep the smallest set whose total reaches at least p; drop the rest
divide the kept probabilities by their total and sample one at random
the kept set's size adapts to confidence, unlike a fixed k
it only removes the tail; it doesn't sharpen or flatten the rest (that's temperature)
it's a chosen setting, not a rule: greedy often matches it when you need just one answer

retrieve.q: Explain why a top-p cut suits pass@k-style evaluation better than either greedy decoding or sampling from the full distribution.
answer: greedy gives the same program every time, so extra samples add nothing
full sampling occasionally picks a junk token, and a long program has many chances to hit one
top-p keeps randomness among the plausible tokens and removes only the tail

retrieve.q: Using the card's bars, redo the cut for p = 0.9 instead of 0.95: how many tokens survive, what do you divide by, and what probability does total end up with?
answer: running totals 0.40, 0.70, 0.85, 0.92: 0.92 is the first ≥ 0.9, so 4 tokens survive (evens is cut too)
divide by 0.92
total becomes 0.40 / 0.92 ≈ 0.435 (was 0.4167 at p = 0.95)

retrieve.q: A model assigns 0.90 to one token and splits the remaining 0.10 over four others (0.04, 0.03, 0.02, 0.01). Compare what top-3 and top-p 0.9 keep, and say which behaviour you want here and why.
answer: top-3 keeps 3 tokens (0.90, 0.04, 0.03): the two runner-ups still get about 4% and 3% after rescaling
top-p 0.9 keeps just the one token, because 0.90 alone reaches p
when the model is sure, you usually want the sure token; a fixed k keeps options it doesn't believe in

retrieve.q: When would you not bother with top-p, and what would you use instead?
answer: when only one answer is needed: greedy often does as well (pass@1-style use)
when a grammar mask is active and a valid token might sit in the tail (mask first, or turn top-p off)
it's a popular default, not a guaranteed winner; some evaluations use temperature alone or top-k

compare.q: Temperature and top-p both change how varied Codex's samples are. What does each one do to the distribution, and why does Codex tune temperature per k but leave p fixed at 0.95?
answer: temperature rescales every logit: it keeps all tokens but moves mass toward (low T) or away from (high T) the favourite
top-p keeps the order and ratios but zeroes the tail
temperature is the diversity dial matched to the budget (0.2 for pass@1, 0.8 for pass@100); top-p is a safety cut that stays useful at any T
failure modes: T too high lets junk rise; top-p alone can't make samples sharper

compare.q: Under a JSON grammar, top-p 0.9 can leave zero valid tokens. What property of top-p causes that, and what order of operations fixes it?
answer: top-p cuts by probability rank, blind to validity
if the only valid token (} at 2%) is in the tail, the cut removes it and the mask then leaves nothing
apply the grammar mask first, then top-p on what's left; or turn top-p off for strict schemas

compare.q: The bigram sampler draws from the full distribution with torch.multinomial. What would a top-p cut change in its output, and what would it cost?
answer: same draw, but over a sorted, truncated and renormalised row
rare transitions (like the 0.0065 e → x step in the card's walk) would often be cut, so fewer odd names
the cost: less variety, and a model that samples only from the head no longer reflects the full distribution it learned

predict.q: Take the card's eight tokens as the whole distribution and apply temperature 0.5 before the p = 0.95 cut. Does the nucleus grow, shrink, or stay at 5 tokens? Commit, then reveal.
predict.answer: It shrinks to 3. Squaring each probability (T = 0.5) and renormalising gives about 0.572, 0.322, 0.081, 0.018, …, so total, return and result already reach 0.975. At T = 2 the opposite happens: the distribution flattens and 7 of the 8 tokens survive. Temperature sets how far the mass is spread; top-p then decides how much of it to keep.

apply.task: By hand, apply top-p to the card's distribution for p = 0.95, 0.9 and 0.7. For each, list the kept tokens and the rescaled probability of total. Then write a 10-line top_p(probs, p) function (sort, running total, cut, divide) and check it reproduces your three answers. Edge case: at p = 0.7 the running total hits exactly 0.70. Does your code keep 2 tokens or 3?
apply.done: Your function gives 5 tokens (total 0.4167), 4 tokens (0.4348) and 2 tokens (0.5714), and uses "at least p" (≥), so p = 0.7 keeps exactly 2.
apply.hint: Break on the first index where the running total is ≥ p, and include that token. With floats, 0.40 + 0.30 may not equal 0.70 exactly, so compare against p minus a tiny epsilon.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: how many tokens survive at low temperature, or the top-3 vs top-p count for the confident model?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why rescaling keeps the ratios, or why the cut size follows confidence?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: temperature → spread of mass, or spread of mass → nucleus size?
Could you say, without the chart, why pure sampling gets riskier the longer the program?
Before the sampling-with-grammar card, what would you check about the order in which top-p and a mask run?
